title: Two-colour brioche scarf
subtitle: A reversible two-colour brioche rib that shows different colours on each face.
excerpt: A straight scarf knitted flat in two-colour brioche on 5 mm needles with DK-weight yarn in two contrasting colours, finishing at 22 cm wide by 170 cm long. Each face of the finished scarf shows a dominant colour with the contrast colour visible in the rib valleys, and the colours swap between the two faces. The technique uses alternating single-colour rows, one for each yarn.
sourceNotes: Two-colour brioche stitch derives from Victorian brioche-stitch samplers documented in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive. The modern two-colour approach of alternating yarn rows in brioche was systematised by Nancy Marchant in the early 21st century and draws on the same historical slip-stitch-with-yarn-over principles.
heroPrompt: A two-colour brioche scarf in teal and burnt orange DK yarn, photographed folded to show both faces side by side -- teal dominant on one face, orange dominant on the other.

glossaryTerms.definition: A brioche fabric worked with two yarn colours, each used on alternate rows (one dark row, one light row). The colour that is knitted on a given row dominates the face seen from the knit side, while the colour that is slipped appears in the rib valleys.
Brioche knit: knit the slipped stitch together with its paired yarn-over from the previous row as a single stitch.
Brioche purl: purl the slipped stitch together with its paired yarn-over from the previous row as a single stitch.
Slip one stitch purlwise with the yarn in front, then bring the yarn over the right needle tip to the back. The slip and the yarn-over sit together on the right needle as a paired unit.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a straight scarf knitted flat in
two-colour brioche
on 5 mm needles with DK-weight yarn in two contrasting colours, finishing at 22 cm wide and 170 cm long. Two yarns alternate one row at a time: one colour for the
BrK
(brioche knit) rows and the other for the
BrP

(brioche purl) rows. The face you are looking at shows the colour used on the BrK row, and the other face shows the alternate colour. The scarf is fully reversible with different colours on each face.

Flat construction was chosen because two-colour brioche flat requires joining and dropping each yarn at the end of its row. This is straightforward on straight needles where both yarn ends hang at the same edge. The finished scarf needs about 350 m of each colour (around 120 g each for DK) and wraps around the neck with extra warmth from the two-yarn structure.
What you need

items.name: DK-weight wool or wool-blend yarn, colour A (main colour)
items.substitutions: Any DK-weight yarn. Both yarns must be the same weight for even brioche columns.

items.name: DK-weight wool or wool-blend yarn, colour B (contrast colour)
5 mm needles, circular 80 cm or longer (UK 6 / US 8)
items.substitutions: A long circular makes it easy to slide the work back to the other end without turning.

content.text: Gauge

16 sts x 24 rows = 10 x 10 cm in two-colour brioche on 5 mm needles, unblocked. Two-colour brioche gauge is measured in working stitches only, not counting the yarn-overs on the needle. A two-colour brioche row is half a pattern row: the full stitch count only reads at a two-row mark. Swatch at least 8 cm in the two-colour pattern and measure working stitch columns across the centre. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by about 1.4 cm at this stitch count.
Stitches used
Sl1yo
: bring yarn to front, slip next stitch purlwise, carry yarn over right needle tip to back. The slip and yarn-over sit together as a paired unit.
BrK: insert right needle through slipped stitch and its yarn-over together knitwise, wrap yarn, draw through. One unit consumed.
BrP: bring yarn to front, insert right needle through slipped stitch and its yarn-over together purlwise, wrap yarn, draw through to back. One unit consumed.
Pattern
Cast on
Using colour A and the
long-tail cast-on

, place 38 stitches on the needle. The stitch count must be even. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 5 mm needles (circumference approximately 15.7 mm) and 38 stitches: (15.7 x 38) / 10 + 15 = 59.7 + 15 = about 75 cm. Leave a tail of at least 75 cm.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 38 stitches on the needle.
Body
Set-up row (using colour A, RS facing): K1 (selvedge), *Sl1yo, K1; repeat from * to last stitch, K1 (selvedge). (38 sts)
Note: from this point each row uses only one colour. Colour A is used for the RS rows (BrK rows). Colour B is used for the WS rows (BrP rows). The yarn not in use hangs at the edge.
Row 1 (RS, Colour A): K1, *BrK, Sl1yo(B); repeat from * to last stitch, K1. (38 sts) -- Sl1yo(B) means the colour B stitch is slipped with its yarn-over.
Row 2 (WS, Colour B): K1, *Sl1yo(A), BrP; repeat from * to last stitch, K1. (38 sts)

Repeat rows 1 and 2 until the scarf measures 170 cm from the cast-on. The yarns will alternate at the edges: Colour A hangs at the right end of each RS row and Colour B at the right end of each WS row. Pick up the correct yarn for each row. At the halfway mark (approximately row 203, around 85 cm), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 203 you should have 38 working stitches on the needle.
Bind off

Work a stretchy bind-off using colour A on a RS row: BrK the first brioche stitch, *slip resulting stitch back to left needle, K2tog through back loops; repeat from * to end. Cut both yarns, weave in all four tails.
Common faults

Colours mixing on one face. Each colour should appear on only one face. If a colour bleeds to the wrong face, you picked up the wrong yarn for that row. Check which colour you are holding before beginning each row.

Yarn tangles at the edge. The two yarns cross at the edge of every row. Keep them on separate yarn bobbins or in two separate yarn bowls placed on the same side of your chair. Untwist the strands every 20 rows or so.

Stitch count rising. The sl1yo unit must be consumed by the following BrK or BrP on the next row. If a sl1yo is worked twice without being consumed, the count rises. Always check that each sl1yo from the previous row is worked as a BrK or BrP on the current row.

Edges tangling where yarns are picked up. The yarn not in use must be carried loosely up the selvedge edge. Do not pull it tight. A loose carry keeps the edge elastic and prevents the scarf from narrowing at the selvedge.
Finishing
Weave in all four tails (two cast-on, two bind-off) separately along the back of the selvedge edge, one tail per colour column. Trim close.
Two-colour brioche does not benefit from wet blocking, which can flatten the loft permanently. Lay flat to settle the rib and leave the piece unstretched.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Press out water gently and lay flat to dry. Do not wring or stretch the brioche rib lengthwise while damp.
What to try next

The brioche cowl applies the same two-colour technique in the round. The yarn management differs but the BrK and BrP operations are the same. The two-colour ribbed cowl is simpler if you want a reversible two-colour fabric without the brioche complexity.
